questions: Which two forces act on the block, and in which directions?
Why does the block keep sliding even though friction is acting?
segments.say: Friction opposes relative motion. Watch the block: a 60-newton push drives it right, then the friction arrow grows at the contact at 40 newtons, pointing back against the slide. Do the subtraction with me: 60 take away 40 leaves a net 20 newtons, so the block keeps sliding. Keep your student notes open at the friction and net force definitions for this scene.

questions: Why does the lighter weight balance the heavier one once it slides outward?
What moment must each side reach for this beam to balance?
segments.say: Moments: force times distance from the pivot. On the left, 60 newtons at half a metre makes 30 newton-metres. On the right, 30 newtons at 0.75 metres makes only 22.5, so the beam tips left - then watch the right weight slide out to a full metre: 30 times 1.0 is 30, the moments match, and the beam levels. Now try the moment question on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: What changed between the two readings - the force, or the area?
If the area halved instead of falling to a tenth, what would the pressure become?
segments.say: Pressure: the same force on different areas. The crate weighs 200 newtons and rests on half a square metre: 200 over 0.5 is 400 pascals. Now watch it tip onto its narrow edge - the force is still 200 newtons, but the area is now 0.05 square metres, so the pressure is 4000 pascals and the dent deepens. Check the pressure rule in your student notes.

questions: In which direction does the tyre push on the road, and in which direction does friction push on the tyre?
Why is it wrong to say friction always opposes motion?
segments.say: Check the thinking. The driving wheel rolls forward, but its contact patch pushes backward on the road - so the road pushes back, and friction on the tyre points forward: friction drives the car. It opposes the relative slide, never the motion itself. Then take the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits the tiptoe claim head-on.
segments.watchFor: The same push gives the same pressure whether you stand flat or on tiptoes. Listen for it in pair talk and watch for it on the exit ticket: The push feels the same, so the effect on the ground feels like it should be the same. Send them back to the crate tipping onto its narrow edge and the correct turn: Pressure is force over area: tiptoes spread the same force over a smaller area, so the pressure is higher.
